blocks.text: Four parts build the case for the strategy in Chapter 3. Section 2.1 draws lessons from comparator destinations; sections 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4 then examine demand, supply and the enabling environment, on which Pillars 1, 2 and 3 rest.

Demand is not what holds the province back. Its shape and the system that serves it do. Five markets and six months carry most overseas visits, and seats into Cape Town run out at the peak. Beyond the Metro, product is hard to reach and book, and in townships and rural settlements the missing piece is a local seller. The institutions that should hold the system together have thinned. Section 2.1 first shows how the fastest growers dealt with their own binding constraint.

Stakeholder evidence runs through sections 2.2 to 2.4. The first of four engagement phases ran from January to March 2026 (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p4, p17; the record of the three later phases is not yet in hand). In it, 16 organisations from Mossel Bay to the CTICC gave 223 rated insights: 115 High, 102 Medium and 6 Low (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p20 to p46, counted). Each stakeholder statement in this chapter is the project team's paraphrase of a point an organisation made, attributed to that organisation and never to a person. [Open item: each organisation named here to approve its paraphrase before publication.] Each part ends with a box, "What this means for the strategy". The box says what the evidence does to the focus areas it touches: it validates, rewords, refines, adds, flags or supports them, or supplies precedent or evidence.
2.1 Global benchmarks and their lessons

The destinations that grew fastest ran institutions, marketing and air access as one system aimed at a single binding constraint. For the Western Cape that constraint is seats into one gateway; in its townships and rural settlements it is the lack of a local seller.

The six comparators are Chile; Melbourne and Victoria; Valencia; Singapore; Kenya; and Auckland and New Zealand (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p12; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p62; an earlier baseline had proposed adding Namibia and Kenya, and the final set kept Kenya only). They came from a screen of 30 destinations against 12 criteria in four groups: market and access; destination and product structure; growth and inclusion; performance (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p11, p12). Each case was read for its demand profile, two proven growth levers and how far they transfer to the Western Cape (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p13; examples from outside the set are cited as public sources and labelled as such). Growth of 3% to 5% a year is the norm under stable conditions; above 5% marks structural acceleration and 10% or more a structural shift (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p7). UN Tourism puts global growth at 11% in 2024, while recovery was still running, and about 4% in 2025 (World Tourism Barometer, Jan 2025 and Jan 2026). Growth counts as structural only when it is "driven by deliberate changes to demand drivers, access conditions or product systems, rather than cyclical recovery or short-term promotion" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p8).
Fast growth in 2024 was partly recovery

Only Chile and Singapore grew far faster than the world in 2024. Chile grew 40.4% and Singapore 21%, two to four times the world's 11% (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p9; Sernatur, Dec 2025; Singapore Tourism Board, Feb 2025). Neither rate proves structural growth. Singapore was still at 86% of its 2019 arrivals, and most of Chile's arrivals came overland, 40% of them from Argentina (Sernatur, Dec 2025; Singapore Tourism Board, Feb 2025). Kenya (14.6%), Valencia (13% to 14%) and New Zealand (about 12%) grew only slightly faster than the world. Melbourne's 4.3% is an Australia-wide forecast of average annual growth rather than an actual (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p9, p17, p53; the 12% for New Zealand matches its 2025 holiday-arrivals growth, with total arrivals up 5.9%). The lessons that follow come from what the leaders built over a decade, not from one year's rate.
The Western Cape should apply the same test to its own record: growth counts when deliberate change drives it, not when recovery returns lost visitors (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p8).
Cape Town wins more routes than its peers

Cape Town wins routes faster than its peers. Between 2015 and 2025 it added 17 mainline international services, more than any of eight secondary airports chosen for peripheral geography and inbound tourism (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "International Comparisons"). The eight are Calgary, Christchurch, Edinburgh, Keflavik, Larnaca, Marrakech, Santiago and Valencia. Santiago added 14 services, Valencia 12 and Calgary 8 (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Executive Summary", "International Comparisons"; other study documents count new routes from 2014 on a different basis). Yet winning routes is not the same as holding seats through the winter, and the routes won now run full (section 2.3). The Western Cape does not need to learn how to win routes. It needs what the leaders added: access funded as infrastructure and marketing tied to each route.
The leaders treat air access as infrastructure

Chile, the fastest grower, put access first and treated it as infrastructure. Santiago is Chile's air gateway. Its airport traffic rose from about 16 million passengers in 2010 to more than 26 million in 2019 (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p24, p25; the source prints about 90% to 95% of 5.2 million international arrivals through Santiago, which can hold only for air arrivals, since land borders carried 55.6% in 2024). A private concession won in 2015 funded about US$900 million of expansion, under one of the world's most liberal aviation systems built on open-skies agreements (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p23, p26).

New Zealand made marketing money follow routes. It "shifted from awareness-driven marketing to route accountable demand generation", tying budgets to specific long-haul corridors and designing campaigns around airline breakeven and shoulder-season loads (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p54). The programme reports more than 16,000 incremental bookings and a return of about NZ$55 million in 2023/24. Government-backed early-stage route incentives and data shared between tourism bodies and airlines support it (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p54).

For the Western Cape, the two cases point to three changes. Air access should be treated as "core economic infrastructure, not a tourism add-on", with "a permanent, well-funded Public-Private Air Access Fund" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p28). The province should "actively lobby for air service liberalisation and simplified visa regimes" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p28). Marketing budgets should be ring-fenced around priority long-haul corridors, with an aviation partnership framework and early-stage route support (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p56).
Transit and events can be turned into demand

Hubs can be converted into visits, not just flown through. Singapore does it through its stopover programme, with the tourism board, Changi Airport Group and Singapore Airlines working "under a coordinated strategy" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p40). It received 16.5 million international visitors in 2024 and record tourism receipts of about S$29 billion (Singapore Tourism Board, Feb 2025). Kenya positioned Nairobi as East Africa's aviation, diplomatic and business hub, and its main airport now carries 68% of arrivals (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p32, p34).

Events do the same work across the calendar. Victoria curates a portfolio of events that "generate repeat, predictable demand spikes across the year" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p18). Melbourne "uses its event calendar to de-risk and stimulate aviation demand" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p59). Behind the calendar, hotel stock grew 21%, about 5,000 rooms (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p18).

The province needs one event acquisition and calendar strategy across Wesgro, the Convention Bureau, the City and the Province, with conference bidding aligned to sector strengths (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p20). MICE should be treated as a system lever, with city, provincial and national actors aligned around a gateway strategy (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p35). Government, aviation, events and industry should work to shared KPIs (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p42). The Western Cape already has the hub traffic and the green-season gap that these levers address (section 2.2).
Quality and value are governed, not encouraged

The leaders manage quality and yield as deliberate outcomes. Valencia adopted a destination-wide quality system across its tourism businesses and placed coordination in "a permanent public-private structure led by Visit València" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p47). It received 3.5 million international visitors in 2024, 13.9% more than in 2023 and 24.4% above 2019 (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p46).

New Zealand manages regional capacity to protect pricing and recommends that destinations "replace arrival growth with yield-based regional performance metrics" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p55, p56). Kenya earned about US$1,460 per visitor in 2024 by building conservation and community participation into one governed product system (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p15; Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p32, p33).

For the Western Cape the cases ask first for a province-wide quality and standards framework led by Wesgro (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p42). Within it would sit a provincial quality charter phased by district, with certification "visible across booking platforms" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p49). Standing sector councils for wine, MICE, adventure and culture would sit beside the charter (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p49). The cases also ask the province to measure its regions by yield rather than arrivals and to build conservation and community inclusion into the offer (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p35, p55, p56). Quality, price and yield are managed outcomes, not by-products of volume.
In communities, lasting sellers matter more than capital

In communities the binding constraint is the seller. Five further cases, from Rio de Janeiro to Kliptown, show that local sellers outlast the programmes that launch them (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p7 to p11). In Santa Marta in Rio de Janeiro, about 20 resident guides ran the tours by 2015 and outside jeep firms had left. The guides kept selling after the launch programme ended, while assets and training without a route to market did not last (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p7, p30). Access and safety were preconditions, not product.

Scale brings its own limits. Medellín's Comuna 13 drew 1.98 million visitors in 2025, 52% of them international, with about 300 professional guides. Mobility built for residents became the stage, but carrying-capacity limits came late (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p8). On Vilakazi Street in Soweto, ten restaurants employ more than 800 people. Public space upgrades amplify existing assets, but benefits concentrate on street-front owners (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p9).

Neither capital nor donor money lasts without a seller that can stand alone. Costa Rica's community network turned over more than USD 800,000 in 2013 and dissolved at the end of 2018, after donors left (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p10). A selling entity is the engine and must survive donor exit. Kliptown in Soweto received a first allocation of R436 million and was projected to draw almost 200,000 international visitors a year. By 2017 its museum drew about 4,000 visitors a year, because capital built before an operator yields no operating income (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p11).

The cases converge on one order: "a seller with a stake, a safe and workable visit, product that keeps spend in the community, then exposure" (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p12). In the Western Cape's communities, the seller therefore comes before the asset (section 2.4).
The system matters more than any lever

No single lever explains the leaders' growth. Sustained tourism growth "is not created by fragmented interventions, but by a coordinated destination system in which governance, demand generation and access reinforce one another" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p58). Chile's coordination works best "when anchored around a single strategic constraint", which for Chile was long-haul access (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p59). The Western Cape's constraint has the same shape as Chile's: seats into one gateway airport (section 2.3).

Yet coordination is hard everywhere. Victoria reports tension between national and state bodies over roles and branding (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p16). Valencia struggles to join its data across institutions, and Kenya's collaboration between government, industry and financiers is "mixed" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p31, p45). The Western Cape's three tiers of government show the same strain (section 2.4).
The strategy should follow the same order: peak seats into Cape Town first, one system built around them and, in the communities, a seller before any asset.

blocks.title: What this means for the strategy
paras: **Supplies precedent for FA07, Win direct routes and add seats on full routes, and FA15, Crowd in capital with targeted investment strategies.** Chile's airport concession and air access fund; New Zealand's route-tied marketing.
**Supplies precedent for FA04, Convert India and China hub traffic.** Singapore's joint strategy with its airport and airline, and Kenya's hub strategy.
**Supplies precedent for FA02, Create green-season demand with MICE and events.** Melbourne's events-led system and unified calendar.

**Supplies precedent for FA11, Align visitor experience in-destination, and FA03, Make the whole province findable and bookable.** Valencia's governed quality and certification visible on booking platforms.

**Supplies precedent for FA05, Increase yield in mature markets, FA12, Balance impact on nature-based attractions, and FA14, Manage climate risk and sustainable tourism.** Yield-based metrics, capacity discipline and conservation-led product.

**Supports FA16, Align institutional stakeholders across all three tiers, FA17, Strengthen industry and government collaboration, and FA18, Expedite tourism-enabling policy and data sharing.** One coordinated system of governance, marketing and access, with shared data between tourism bodies and airlines.

**Supplies precedent for FA13, Embed local destination bodies for community inclusion.** Resident sellers outlasted the programmes that launched them, and capital built before an operator, as in Kliptown, earned no operating income.
